slides.title: Binary classification in medicine: the confusion matrix
slides.body:
Most clinical decisions are binary: disease vs not, treat vs not, admit vs discharge.

**Confusion matrix**:
```
              Predicted +    Predicted -
Actual +         TP             FN       (FNR = miss rate)
Actual -         FP             TN       (FPR = false alarm)
```

**Sensitivity (recall, TPR)**: $TP / (TP + FN)$. Probability test correctly identifies disease. Asks: 'if disease present, will test detect it?'

**Specificity (TNR)**: $TN / (TN + FP)$. Probability test correctly excludes. Asks: 'if no disease, will test be negative?'

**Positive Predictive Value (PPV, precision)**: $TP / (TP + FP)$. Asks: 'if test positive, is disease present?'

**Negative Predictive Value (NPV)**: $TN / (TN + FN)$. Asks: 'if test negative, is disease absent?'

**Critical**: PPV + NPV depend on PREVALENCE (base rate). Sensitivity + specificity don't.

**Bayes' theorem in clinical terms**:
$$\text{Posterior probability of disease} = \text{prior} \times \text{Likelihood Ratio}$$

**Likelihood Ratios (LRs)**:
- $LR^+ = \text{sens} / (1 - \text{spec})$. How much positive test raises probability.
- $LR^- = (1 - \text{sens}) / \text{spec}$. How much negative test lowers probability.
- LR+ > 10 strongly raises probability. LR− < 0.1 strongly lowers.

**Diagnostic odds = pre-test odds × LR**.

**Prevalence affects PPV dramatically**:
- Test: sens 99%, spec 99%. Prevalence 0.1% (rare disease).
  - PPV ≈ sens × prev / (sens × prev + (1-spec) × (1-prev)) = 0.99 × 0.001 / (0.99 × 0.001 + 0.01 × 0.999) ≈ 9%.
  - 91% of positives are FALSE positives despite excellent test!
- Same test, prevalence 20% (common): PPV ≈ 96%.
- This is why mass screening for rare conditions is hard. Most positives are false.

The **interactive ROC viz below** lets you explore these dynamics. Drag class separation, prevalence, threshold. Watch the confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV update. Notice: at low prevalence, even a great-AUC test has low PPV.

slides.title: ROC + AUC + calibration
slides.body:
**ROC curve (Receiver Operating Characteristic)**: plot of TPR (sensitivity) vs FPR (1 − specificity) at all possible thresholds.

**Reading the ROC**:
- (0,0): always negative. No false alarms, no detections.
- (1,1): always positive. Catches all but maximum false alarms.
- (0,1): perfect classifier. All positives detected, no false alarms.
- Diagonal: random guessing.
- Curve in upper-left = good.

**AUC (Area Under ROC)**:
- 0.5 = random.
- 1.0 = perfect.
- 0.7-0.8 = decent.
- 0.8-0.9 = good.
- 0.9+ = excellent.
- AUC = probability that a randomly chosen positive ranks higher than a randomly chosen negative.

**AUC limitations**:
- Insensitive to threshold choice; can mask bad calibration.
- Single number obscures performance at clinically-relevant thresholds.
- Doesn't account for prevalence in clinical context.

**PR (Precision-Recall) curve**: alternative for highly imbalanced data (rare disease). Plots precision (PPV) vs recall (sensitivity). AUPRC is the metric.

**Calibration**: predicted probability matches observed frequency.
- Well-calibrated: when model says 30% risk, ~30% of those patients have outcome.
- Mis-calibrated: model says 30% but actual is 60% (under-confident) or 10% (over-confident).
- **Reliability diagram**: plot predicted vs observed in bins.
- **Brier score**: mean squared error of probabilities. Lower better.
- **Hosmer-Lemeshow test**: traditional calibration test. Now often deprecated for poor power.
- **Calibration slope + intercept**: from logistic regression of outcome on logit(prediction). Slope = 1, intercept = 0 = perfect.

**Recalibration**:
- **Platt scaling**: fit logistic regression on validation set.
- **Isotonic regression**: monotonic + non-parametric.
- **Temperature scaling**: simple one-parameter for deep learning models.

**Why calibration matters more than AUC in clinical contexts**:
- Decisions made at specific risk thresholds (e.g., 'treat if >10% risk').
- Mis-calibration leads to wrong action.
- Risk communication: '10% chance of stroke' should be ~10% to be useful.
- AUC can be high while calibration is poor (especially in deep learning).

**Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI)**: when comparing two models, how many patients are correctly re-categorized? Risk-based clinical metric.

**Decision-curve analysis** (Vickers): plot net benefit vs threshold probability. Considers FN cost vs FP cost across thresholds. More clinically useful than ROC alone.

slides.title: Threshold selection + NNT + clinical utility
slides.body:
**Threshold selection**: where on the ROC curve do you operate?

Depends on:
- **Relative cost of FN vs FP**.
- **Prevalence**.
- **Downstream actions**.

**Examples**:
- **Sepsis screening**: high sensitivity (don't miss sepsis); FPs lead to alerts that can be silenced. Threshold low.
- **Cancer screening**: balance sensitivity (don't miss cancer) + specificity (don't over-biopsy). Often biopsy threshold ~5-15% predicted risk.
- **MRI in suspected MS**: very specific (treatment is long-term + serious). Threshold high.
- **Trauma triage**: high sensitivity (don't miss life threats); accept many FPs.

**Operating point**: specific (sens, spec) chosen for deployment.

**Net Reclassification + decision-analytic frameworks** help formalize.

**Number Needed to Treat (NNT)**:
$$NNT = 1 / ARR$$
Where $ARR$ = absolute risk reduction. NNT = patients needed to treat to prevent one bad outcome.

- Low NNT (~5-10): very effective.
- Moderate (10-50): typical.
- High (100+): marginal at population scale; can still be valuable.

**Examples**:
- Statins primary prevention: NNT ~50-100 (prevent one CV event over 5 years).
- ACE inhibitors in heart failure: NNT ~20.
- Vaccine: NNT to prevent severe COVID ~20-50 in elderly.
- Aspirin for MI prevention (low-risk patient): NNT ~1000+ → outweighed by bleed risk.

**Number Needed to Harm (NNH)**: patients needed to cause one adverse event.

**NNT vs NNH ratio** drives clinical decisions.

**Clinical utility validation**:
- **Discrimination** (AUC).
- **Calibration**.
- **Clinical impact**: does using the model improve outcomes vs standard of care?
- Last point often unmeasured. AI tools that improve AUC may not improve patient outcomes (workflow disruption, alert fatigue, false reassurance).

**Prospective trial vs retrospective**:
- Retrospective: develop + test on historical data. Cheap, fast, biased.
- Prospective: deploy + measure outcomes. Expensive, slow, true validation.
- Most FDA-approved AI: retrospective validation. Few have RCTs showing clinical benefit.
- Active discussion: should clinical AI require RCT-level evidence? FDA evolving frameworks.

**The 'shift to action'**: clinical AI that helps action is more valuable than pure prediction. Real-time, actionable, integrated with workflow. EXAMPLES:
- Viz.ai stroke triage: directly alerts neurointerventionalist for LVO; demonstrated reduced time-to-thrombectomy.
- Sepsis early-warning: shown reduced mortality in some implementations + caused alert fatigue in others.

**Real-world impact**: most clinical AI does NOT have rigorous outcome evidence. Field maturing rapidly toward outcomes-based evaluation.

question.question: Compute PPV given prevalence
question.goal: Diagnostic test: sensitivity 95%, specificity 90%. Apply to a population with disease prevalence 1%.

steps.prompt: Set up: 10,000 patients × 1% prevalence = 100 with disease, 9,900 without. Apply test. True positives = ?
False positives among the 9,900 without disease?

steps.reveal: PPV ≈ 8.8%. Despite 95% sensitivity + 90% specificity, only 8.8% of positives are true positives! 91.2% are false positives. Mass screening for rare conditions is treacherous.

steps.prompt: Compare at prevalence 20% (common): same test, what's PPV?
steps.reveal: PPV ≈ 70.4%. SAME TEST, PPV 8.8% → 70.4% as prevalence rises from 1% to 20%. Bayesian logic. Prevalence dominates PPV.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{PPV depends on prevalence: high-sens/spec test still has low PPV at low prevalence}}$$ The 'paradox of mass screening for rare disease': even excellent tests can yield mostly false positives. Why HIV screening in low-prevalence groups requires confirmatory testing; why cancer-screening recommendations focus on high-prevalence populations; why Bayes' theorem is everywhere in clinical reasoning. Modern ML doesn't change this — calibration is essential to communicate appropriate uncertainty.

question.question: Two cancer-screening models have identical AUC = 0.85. Which would you prefer?
options: Need more info: prefer one with better CALIBRATION + better performance AT THE CLINICALLY-RELEVANT THRESHOLD (e.g., 5% risk for screening decision). AUC is single-number summary; clinical decisions made at specific thresholds. Better calibration + better sens/spec at deployment threshold matter more than aggregate AUC.
question.explanation:
AUC = aggregate metric across ALL thresholds. Two models with same AUC can have very different performance at the clinically-relevant threshold. Plus: deep-learning models often have HIGH AUC + POOR CALIBRATION (over- or under-confident).

For clinical use: check (1) sens + spec at deployment threshold; (2) calibration (reliability diagram, Brier score); (3) decision-curve analysis (net benefit). Better single-number summary: AUC + calibration + threshold-specific metrics.

Real-world: many published clinical AI papers report only AUC. Re-evaluation often reveals poor calibration or threshold-specific issues. The field is maturing toward better evaluation standards (TRIPOD-AI, CONSORT-AI).

slides.workedSolution: AUC = aggregate; clinical decisions at specific thresholds. AUC same → very different threshold-specific performance possible. Calibration: critical for risk communication + decisions. Decision-curve analysis: net benefit across thresholds. TRIPOD-AI + CONSORT-AI = newer reporting standards emphasizing this. Prefer model with better calibration + better performance at clinically relevant threshold.

question.question: Drug reduces 5-year MI risk from 10% to 7%. NNT?
Sepsis early-warning AI
question.prompt: Your hospital deploys an AI that predicts sepsis 6 hours before clinical onset. Sensitivity 75%, specificity 85%. Walk through the impact on workflow + outcomes + alert fatigue.
Explain in two or three sentences why CALIBRATION matters more than AUC for clinical decision-support.
question.rubric: Mentions that clinical decisions are made at specific risk thresholds + require accurate risk communication; well-calibrated 10% prediction should mean 10% actual; high-AUC models can be poorly calibrated (especially deep learning); recalibration (Platt, isotonic, temperature scaling) often necessary. AUC ranks; calibration enables risk-based action.
